title: Church hurt
hook: many have been wounded by Christians; healing may take time and distance

segments.voice: Yesterday, when the church does wrong: judgment begins at the house of God, and Zacchaeus paid it back fourfold. Your line was repent. Did you make one plain apology, with no excuses attached? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-five.

A woman drives past the church she grew up in. Same red door. Same sign out front with the sermon title in plastic letters. She hasn't been inside for years, and her stomach still tightens at the sight of it. Somebody in there once told her something about herself, and about God, that she's still trying to unhear. Friends ask now and then when she'll go back, as if it were a cold she ought to be over by now. Some people carry wounds that came from Christians, in a place that was meant to be safe. Today: church hurt.

The prophet Ezekiel has a whole chapter on this. God speaks against the shepherds of Israel, the leaders who were meant to care for the people, and the charges are specific: "The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken." Then the verdict: "with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them." Notice whose side the text is on. It doesn't scold the sheep for scattering. Then God says what he will do himself: "I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken." Driven away. The text knows that some sheep didn't wander off. They were pushed. Next, Matthew, borrowing Isaiah's words to describe Jesus: "A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench." A reed already bent. A lamp wick barely smoking. It's a picture of care that goes slowly with damaged things, that won't snap them to make a point. And the Teacher in Ecclesiastes, listing the seasons of a life, includes this one: "a time to heal." In the text, healing has its own season, and it isn't rushed. For some people healing means going back to church, sometimes a different one. For some it means a long season away. Some never go back. Some readers draw a gentle way of standing beside a hurt person from these texts: no rushing, no arguing them back, no turning their pain into a debate about defending the institution. Bind up, and let them set the pace.
screen: `A BRUISED REED SHALL HE NOT BREAK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be gentle with someone church-hurt. Settle, and breathe. Suppose a friend sits down across from you and says, a church hurt me. Notice the first thing you want to say: an explanation, a defense, a story about a good church you know. Set it down, the way you'd set down a heavy bag. Then stay in the scene, just listening, not steering. If the friend is you, listen to yourself the same way. If you pray, you can ask that they be bound up gently, at their own pace. The bell holds the time.
Church hurt. Wounds that come from a church or from Christians. In Ezekiel, God sides with the sheep that were driven away.
Your line: healing takes time. Today, if someone tells you about a church that hurt them, listen all the way to the end without defending anyone. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Some Christians who have been hurt in church step away for a season, find a different congregation, or work through it with a counselor or a trusted pastor; some churches run listening sessions or support for people who were harmed.

fork.setup: in Ezekiel 34, the sheep are scattered, some of them driven away by their own shepherds. what does God say he will do?
options: blame the sheep for wandering off.
seek them, bring them back, and bind up the broken.
leave them to find their own way home.
fork.reveal: "I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken." the anger falls on the shepherds, not the sheep.

original.note: Hebrew: to heal — from "a time to heal" in Ecclesiastes 3:3.

trapdoor: what you thought: church hurt means someone was too sensitive.
what it means: Ezekiel's God sides with the sheep that were driven away, and charges the shepherds who ruled with force and cruelty.
what a scholar hears: Matthew applies Isaiah's bruised reed and smoking flax to Jesus: a care that won't snap what's already bent.

notes: Index hook says 'many have been wounded by Christians'; the lesson avoids the 'many' claim ('some people carry wounds'). Keeper may want to soften the index hook.
Ezekiel 34 is addressed to Israel's rulers ('shepherds of Israel'); the lesson applies it by analogy to church leaders. Confirm the application is fair.
Matthew 12:18–21 quotes Isaiah 42:1–4; 'borrowing Isaiah's words' is the lesson's phrasing.
The hook's scene is invented and names no church or tradition.
Original: לִרְפּוֹא ('to heal') in Ecclesiastes 3:3; confirm spelling and pointing.
Audit: softened narrator assertions ('nobody else gets to set its calendar'; a run of imperatives) into what readers draw from the texts.
Editor pass: rewrote the practice opening so it no longer repeats day 1394's "bring to mind people hurt by a church... maybe yourself".
